title: Amenability to mathematical analysis implies deviations from randomness

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Amenability to mathematical analysis implies deviations from randomness

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The very possibility of detailed mathematical analysis of a system tends to imply that its output has at least some deviations from perfect randomness, whereas simple rules not constrained by the need for such analysis can generate highly random behavior.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the very possibility of any detailed mathematical analysis tends to imply the presence of at least some deviations from perfect randomness.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 7, “Mechanisms in Programs and Nature”; section “The Intrinsic Generation of Randomness” (from p. 315), p. 321. Scope: deterministic systems used to generate randomness, including pseudorandom generators

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch07-08: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.44

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A selected generator corpus can test a proxy correlation, but the proposed implication is vague and selection-sensitive. Existing tests cannot establish the absence of all deviations, so only restricted versions are resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define mathematical amenability using prespecified proof or complexity indicators and randomness by held-out statistical and compression tests, then compare a registered sample of generators. A lack of association or analytically tractable generator passing all strong tests would challenge the tendency.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Every deterministic finite generator has some mathematical description.

Failure to detect deviation is not perfect randomness.

Amenability to analysis has no objective scale.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data existence: 0.78
data adequacy: 0.3
discriminating power: 0.26
operationalizability: 0.25

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Linear congruential generators and linear-feedback registers are public, analyzed, and known to carry detectable regularities, so the intended examples can be checked. The sentence says that the possibility of detailed analysis tends to imply a deviation from perfect randomness, and finding such a deviation is largely what detailed analysis means. The example families are testable; the general tendency is not a separate empirical claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Take generator families with published closed-form analyses and test their outputs for proved regularities such as lattices or linear structure. A fully analyzed family that also passed every declared randomness test would challenge the tendency inside that collection.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Detecting a deviation is itself a piece of analysis, so the sentence is close to a tautology.

Tends to states no rate.

A system can be analyzed in one respect and still pass a fixed test battery.
